ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> In brief, participants were recruited through a university subject pool and social media advertisements and asked to complete a chatbot-based narrative interview designed to assess personality and the Big Five Inventory-2 Extra-Short Form (BFI-2-XS) (Soto & John, 2017).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 706 columns across 74 data files.
#### Issues Identified

106 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 74 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 8 Python code files for reproducibility.
-  8 Python files skipped as byte-identical duplicates of another file already in the run.
-  7 of 7 Python scripts ran without error when executed (1 more file is imported by other files, not run on its own).
-  7 installable Python dependencies detected.

summary_table.live_data_statements: In brief, participants were recruited through a university subject pool and social media advertisements and asked to complete a chatbot-based narrative interview designed to assess personality and the Big Five Inventory-2 Extra-Short Form (BFI-2-XS) (Soto & John, 2017).

report: ### Python code
This module also assesses whether the paper's Python code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 8 Python code files.
#### Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first) and numeric filename prefixes. Python has no `source()`-equivalent import-based ordering signal (an `import` loads a module, not the paper's own analysis flow), so that basis never applies here.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:8, File = c("llm_rating_p1.py", "client_config.py", 
"efficiency_gain_summary.py", "generate_inter_domain_correlation_figures.py", 
"generate_question_orders.py", "make_efficiency_gain_figure.py", 
"response_length_sensitivity.py", "make_response_length_figure.py"
), "Runs after" = c("—", "—", "—", "—", "—", "efficiency_gain_summary.py", 
"—", "response_length_sensitivity.py"), Basis = c("numeric", 
"none", "none", "none", "none", "dependency", "none", "dependency"
)), row.names = c(NA, -8L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**7 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `length_adjusted_order_prefix_comparison.csv` to `additional_analysis/outputs/length_adjusted_order_prefix_comparison.csv` (in response_length_sensitivity.py); `top_bottom_5_sd_word_count_summary.csv` to `additional_analysis/outputs/top_bottom_5_sd_word_count_summary.csv` (in response_length_sensitivity.py); `sd_word_count_correlations.csv` to `additional_analysis/outputs/sd_word_count_correlations.csv` (in response_length_sensitivity.py); `top_bottom_5_sd_word_count_summary.csv` to `outputs/top_bottom_5_sd_word_count_summary.csv` (in make_response_length_figure.py); `sd_word_count_correlations.csv` to `outputs/sd_word_count_correlations.csv` (in make_response_length_figure.py); `length_adjusted_order_prefix_comparison.csv` to `outputs/length_adjusted_order_prefix_comparison.csv` (in make_response_length_figure.py); `efficiency_gain_delta_r_summary.csv` to `outputs/efficiency_gain_delta_r_summary.csv` (in make_efficiency_gain_figure.py). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. 4 references matched several files sharing a name and could not be resolved by study group or folder; they were left unrewritten and flagged.
#### Execution

**The Python code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 8 scripts: 7 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. 1 file was not run on its own, because other files import it: client_config.py (by llm_rating_p1.py). Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions (e.g. in a `requirements.txt`). **2 scripts stopped on a file another script writes**, so they were run once more after the other scripts: `response_length_sensitivity.py` (top_bottom_5_sd_word_count_summary.csv, sd_word_count_correlations.csv); `make_response_length_figure.py` (length_adjusted_order_prefix_comparison.csv). 3 files were written in another folder than where the script looked, so before that run we copied them there: `interview_shortening_code.zip/interview_shortening_code/additional_analysis/outputs/outputs/top_bottom_5_sd_word_count_summary.csv` to `interview_shortening_code.zip/interview_shortening_code/additional_analysis/outputs/additional_analysis/outputs/top_bottom_5_sd_word_count_summary.csv` for `response_length_sensitivity.py`; `interview_shortening_code.zip/interview_shortening_code/additional_analysis/outputs/outputs/sd_word_count_correlations.csv` to `interview_shortening_code.zip/interview_shortening_code/additional_analysis/outputs/additional_analysis/outputs/sd_word_count_correlations.csv` for `response_length_sensitivity.py`; `interview_shortening_code.zip/interview_shortening_code/additional_analysis/outputs/additional_analysis/outputs/length_adjusted_order_prefix_comparison.csv` to `interview_shortening_code.zip/interview_shortening_code/additional_analysis/outputs/outputs/length_adjusted_order_prefix_comparison.csv` for `make_response_length_figure.py`. The scripts assume they all run from one folder; saying which, or building paths from the top of the project (as with `here::here()`), solves this. Then these ran to the end: `response_length_sensitivity.py`, `make_response_length_figure.py`. Which script must run first can be stated in a README, or shown by numbering the file names (01_, 02_). **3 scripts looked for 4 files in another folder than the deposit has them**, so before running them once more we copied them there: `interview_shortening_code.zip/interview_shortening_code/additional_analysis/outputs/efficiency_gain_delta_r_summary.csv` to `interview_shortening_code.zip/interview_shortening_code/additional_analysis/outputs/outputs/efficiency_gain_delta_r_summary.csv` for `make_efficiency_gain_figure.py`; `interview_shortening_code.zip/interview_shortening_code/additional_analysis/outputs/length_adjusted_order_prefix_comparison.csv` to `interview_shortening_code.zip/interview_shortening_code/additional_analysis/outputs/additional_analysis/outputs/length_adjusted_order_prefix_comparison.csv` for `response_length_sensitivity.py`; `interview_shortening_code.zip/interview_shortening_code/additional_analysis/outputs/top_bottom_5_sd_word_count_summary.csv` to `interview_shortening_code.zip/interview_shortening_code/additional_analysis/outputs/outputs/top_bottom_5_sd_word_count_summary.csv` for `make_response_length_figure.py`; `interview_shortening_code.zip/interview_shortening_code/additional_analysis/outputs/sd_word_count_correlations.csv` to `interview_shortening_code.zip/interview_shortening_code/additional_analysis/outputs/outputs/sd_word_count_correlations.csv` for `make_response_length_figure.py`. info.title: Running Head: SEMANTIC INDICES FOR INTERVIEW OPTIMIZATION Optimizing Open-Ended Interview Assessment Using Response-Based Semantic Indices

author.affiliation:
Department of Computer Science
								Johns Hopkins University

Departments of Psychology and Statistics
								University of Illinois
								
									Urbana-Champaign

Department of Psychological Sciences
								Rice University

text.text: We have no known conflicts of interest to disclose.
Ethical Considerations: No new data were collected for this study, and all analyses were conducted on an existing de-identified archival dataset.
Consent to Participate: Not applicable.

Interviews are widely used in personnel selection and psychological assessment because they elicit rich, contextualized responses about individuals' experiences, reasoning, and behavior (Campion et al., 1997; Hough & Oswald, 2000).
text.formatted: Interviews are widely used in personnel selection and psychological assessment because they elicit rich, contextualized responses about individuals' experiences, reasoning, and behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Campion et al., 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Hough & Oswald, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: However, a central challenge in interview-based assessment is maintaining reliability and validity within the limits of respondents' attention and cognitive resources.
Compared to choice-based questionnaires, interviews place greater demands on respondents to recall experiences, organize information, and formulate open-ended responses.
As a result, the quality of interview data depends in part on the effort respondents can sustain across the assessment.
This constraint creates a tension between construct coverage and respondent burden.
Construct validity requires that an assessment has adequate content coverage (Jebb et al., 2021; Messick, 1987; Podsakoff et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Construct validity requires that an assessment has adequate content coverage <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Jebb et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Messick, 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Podsakoff et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In interviews, this often motivates the inclusion of multiple questions targeting different aspects of the intended construct.
At the same time, as interviews lengthen, respondents tend to provide shorter, less informative, and less distinctive answers (Porter et al., 2004; Schmidt et al., 2020).
text.formatted: At the same time, as interviews lengthen, respondents tend to provide shorter, less informative, and less distinctive answers <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Porter et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Schmidt et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, adding more questions does not necessarily yield more useful information, as gains in coverage may be offset by declines in response quality.

In choice-based scale development, item-reduction methods identify items that capture construct-relevant variance while minimizing redundancy (e.g., Boateng et al., 2018; Hinkin, 1995; Smith et al., 2000).
text.formatted: In choice-based scale development, item-reduction methods identify items that capture construct-relevant variance while minimizing redundancy (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Boateng et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Hinkin, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Smith et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: In interview contexts, similar decisions are often guided by expert judgment.
For example, Van Iddekinge et al. (2005) developed a personality-based interview by iteratively refining items and retaining questions that showed agreement among trained raters.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr">Van Iddekinge et al. (2005)</ref> developed a personality-based interview by iteratively refining items and retaining questions that showed agreement among trained raters.

text.text: Although expert judgment is essential, it can be time-intensive and may vary across raters.

Traditional psychometric methods, such as item-total correlations, factor analysis, and item response theory, provide more standardized item-level criteria for item selection (DeVellis & Thorpe, 2021; Hinkin, 1995), but they generally require choice-based responses in structured numerical format.
text.formatted: Traditional psychometric methods, such as item-total correlations, factor analysis, and item response theory, provide more standardized item-level criteria for item selection <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(DeVellis & Thorpe, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Hinkin, 1995)</ref>, but they generally require choice-based responses in structured numerical format.

text.text: Applying these methods to open-ended interviews typically requires coding responses into quantitative data, which introduces additional complexity, cost, and potential sources of error.
Advances in natural language processing (NLP) offer a complementary source of question-level evidence by extracting semantic patterns in interview responses.

From this perspective, questions that consistently elicit responses semantically aligned with the target construct may provide stronger construct-relevant evidence, whereas questions whose responses overlap with those elicited by other questions may contribute less distinctive information.

Prior work has used semantic similarity to examine redundancy and structure among items in choicebased questionnaires (e.g., Milano et al., 2025), showing that embedding-based methods can recover theoretically meaningful patterns of similarity and redundancy from item wording.
text.formatted: Prior work has used semantic similarity to examine redundancy and structure among items in choicebased questionnaires (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Milano et al., 2025)</ref>, showing that embedding-based methods can recover theoretically meaningful patterns of similarity and redundancy from item wording.

text.text: The present study introduces a response-based semantic framework for evaluating openended interview questions.
By response-based, we mean that question-level evidence is computed from narrative responses collected in a development sample, rather than from question wording itself.
In the case study below, this development sample is an archival chatbot-interview dataset.
In future applications, researchers could compute the same indices from pilot responses gathered from the intended population.
The resulting indices are then used to support interview design and refinement before an interview is shortened or revised.
In practice, they can help distinguish questions that are worth retaining from those that add little new information or may need revision.

In our case study, optimized orderings reached 80% of their observed peak convergent validity with no more than 12 of the 34 questions, and redundancy-penalized ordering was generally associated with lower heterotrait correlations at shorter interview lengths.
Efforts to shorten assessments have a long history in psychometrics.

Traditional shortform development relies on structured numerical response data and criteria such as internal consistency, factor loadings, item-total correlations, and item information (Supplemental Material A, Table A1, for an overview).
text.formatted: Traditional shortform development relies on structured numerical response data and criteria such as internal consistency, factor loadings, item-total correlations, and item information (Supplemental Material A, Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">A1</ref>, for an overview).

text.text: Some methods combine multiple criteria within optimization procedures (e.g., Leite et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Some methods combine multiple criteria within optimization procedures (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Leite et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: These procedures are well suited to choicebased questionnaires but cannot be applied directly to open-ended interviews unless narrative responses are first coded or scored.

Open-ended responses can contain rich information about respondents' goals, values, emotions, and habitual patterns of behavior, but this information is not directly available to conventional item-level statistics.
One established approach is human content analysis, in which narrative responses are progressively condensed and organized into codes and categories.
This process can be time-consuming, particularly when the volume of text is large (Erlingsson & Brysiewicz, 2017).
text.formatted: This process can be time-consuming, particularly when the volume of text is large <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Erlingsson & Brysiewicz, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Computational text analysis offers another route by representing narratives numerically.
NLP methods can encode responses as vectors, enabling comparisons between responses and construct definitions and among responses elicited by different questions.
NLP-based methods have been used to infer personality and other psychological constructs from written and spoken language.

Research using social media language has demonstrated that linguistic patterns can recover meaningful individual differences (Park et al., 2015), and subsequent work has examined the psychometric and validity issues involved in language-based personality assessment (Tay et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Research using social media language has demonstrated that linguistic patterns can recover meaningful individual differences <ref type="bibr">(Park et al., 2015)</ref>, and subsequent work has examined the psychometric and validity issues involved in language-based personality assessment <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Tay et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: More recent studies have extended this approach to free-text and interview responses collected through chatbots and automated video interviews (Fan et al., 2023; Hickman et al., 2022; Sylvara et al., 2026).
text.formatted: More recent studies have extended this approach to free-text and interview responses collected through chatbots and automated video interviews <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Fan et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Hickman et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Sylvara et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Across these applications, language-derived scores have shown at least modest convergence with self-reported personality scores.
The primary objective of this literature, however, has been to assess respondents rather than to evaluate the questions that elicited their responses.

Related research has used semantic representations of predefined assessment content to inform item evaluation and scale development. Hsu et al. (2018) derived semantic features from multiple-choice item stems and response options to estimate item difficulty. Kilmen and Bulut (2025) generated embeddings from the item statements of a choice-based questionnaire and used inter-item semantic similarity to select a shorter form. Guenole and Samo (2024) similarly used language embeddings to approximate item discrimination before response data were collected.
text.formatted: Related research has used semantic representations of predefined assessment content to inform item evaluation and scale development. <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Hsu et al. (2018)</ref> derived semantic features from multiple-choice item stems and response options to estimate item difficulty. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Kilmen and Bulut (2025)</ref> generated embeddings from the item statements of a choice-based questionnaire and used inter-item semantic similarity to select a shorter form. <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Guenole and Samo (2024)</ref> similarly used language embeddings to approximate item discrimination before response data were collected.

text.text: Across these studies, the semantic evidence was derived from item wording or other predefined text rather than from respondents' narratives.
The present study extends this work by shifting the source of question-level evidence from predefined item text to the development-sample narratives elicited by open-ended interview questions.

This response-based perspective makes it possible to evaluate questions in terms of both the alignment of elicited responses with the target construct and the overlap among responses elicited by different questions.

The present study develops a response-based semantic approach for evaluating openended interview questions using narrative responses collected from an archival sample of respondents who completed the full set of candidate interview questions.
This archival sample serves as the development sample from which the question-level semantic indices are derived.

Questions are evaluated in terms of both alignment with the target construct and semantic overlap with previously selected questions; the utility function determines whether that overlap is penalized or rewarded in the resulting question sequence.

We define two response-based indices: semantic discrimination (SD), which reflects the alignment between elicited responses and the target construct, and information coverage (IC), which represents semantic overlap between responses to a candidate question and responses to previously selected questions.

Higher IC values indicate greater overlap with the selected questions, whereas lower values indicate that the candidate contributes more distinctive semantic content relative to the current question set.
The two indices are combined to reorder the questions, prioritizing construct relevance while varying how overlap with previously selected questions is weighted.
This section describes the analytic pipeline used to derive response-based semantic indices, rank interview questions, and evaluate the resulting shortened forms.
The pipeline uses development-sample responses to evaluate how candidate interview questions function.
In this case study, the development sample consists of archival interview responses; in new applications, it would typically consist of pilot responses from the intended population.
The pipeline has four stages.

First, development-sample responses and construct definitions are encoded as embeddings, which are numerical vectors representing the semantic content of each text, so that their semantic similarity can be computed in a common vector space.
Second, the embeddings are used to compute two semantic indices for question selection.
SD is a fixed question-level index that reflects the average alignment between responses to a question and the definition of the target construct.
IC is a conditional index that reflects the average semantic overlap between responses to a candidate question and responses to questions already selected.
Lower IC values indicate that the candidate contributes more distinctive content relative to the current question set.
Third, these indices are combined to generate optimized sequences of interview questions that prioritize construct-relevant questions according to different weighting strategies for semantic overlap.
In other words, questions with higher utility under a given weighting strategy are ranked earlier.
Fourth, shortened forms are defined by selecting the first N questions from each ranked question sequence and concatenating participants' responses in that ranked order.

At each interview length, each optimized condition is compared with same-length prefixes of the original interview order; therefore, differences reflect the combined effect of selected questions and their ordering, except at N = 34, where all conditions contain the same 34 responses and differ only in concatenation order.
For each participant-question response and each target-construct definition, we generated an embedding using a pretrained language model.
The archival responses were used only as model inputs; no model parameters were trained or fine-tuned on these data.
Each response and construct definition was encoded as a numerical vector representing its semantic content.
Because embeddings reflect their pretraining data, the semantic relations they produce should be evaluated for the intended application.
Sentence embeddings are commonly evaluated against human similarity judgments on semantic textual similarity tasks (Cer et al., 2017; Reimers & Gurevych, 2019).
text.formatted: Sentence embeddings are commonly evaluated against human similarity judgments on semantic textual similarity tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Cer et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Reimers & Gurevych, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In this setting, construct experts could rate response-definition alignment, and raters familiar with the target population could judge the similarity of response pairs.
These judgments could then be compared with the corresponding embedding-based estimates.
When relevant groups are adequately represented, researchers should also examine the stability of SD, IC, and question rankings across groups.
Embeddings are context-sensitive numerical representations of text (Devlin et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Embeddings are context-sensitive numerical representations of text <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Devlin et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Within a given embedding space, texts with more similar meanings generally have higher cosine similarity.

Within each embedding space, SD was based on cosine similarities between responses and the target-construct definition, whereas IC was based on cosine similarities between responses to a candidate question and responses to questions already selected.
Both indices were used to evaluate questions rather than to score respondents.

We implemented the pipeline using the distilbert-base-uncased checkpoint (Sanh et al., 2019) and OpenAI's text-embedding-3-large model (OpenAI, 2024) to assess the sensitivity of SD, IC, and the resulting question rankings to the choice of embedding model.
text.formatted: We implemented the pipeline using the distilbert-base-uncased checkpoint <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Sanh et al., 2019</ref>) and OpenAI's text-embedding-3-large model (OpenAI, 2024) to assess the sensitivity of SD, IC, and the resulting question rankings to the choice of embedding model.

text.text: The purpose was not to compare model performance, but to examine the extent to which the question-level patterns and resulting rankings were sensitive to the representation model used.
Additional details about model implementation are provided in Supplemental Material B.
Semantic discrimination (SD) operationalizes construct relevance by estimating how closely the responses to a question align with the definition of the target construct (Guenole & Samo, 2024).
text.formatted: Semantic discrimination (SD) operationalizes construct relevance by estimating how closely the responses to a question align with the definition of the target construct <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Guenole & Samo, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This provides researchers with a metric to evaluate how much construct-relevant content is elicited from each interview question.
For question i in construct domain d, we compute SD as the average cosine similarity between development-sample response embeddings for that question and the embedding of the construct definition.

Formally, for question i in construct domain d, semantic discrimination is defined as: where xip is the embedding of participant p's response to question i in the development sample, td is the embedding of the textual definition of trait d, P is the number of development-sample respondents, and cos(⋅,⋅) denotes cosine similarity.
Higher SD values indicate stronger semantic alignment with the intended construct.

In this sense, SD reflects construct relevance in semantic space, rather than serving as a direct analog of an item discrimination parameter in item response theory (IRT; Embretson & Reise, 2000; see also Supplemental Material A, Table A1).
text.formatted: In this sense, SD reflects construct relevance in semantic space, rather than serving as a direct analog of an item discrimination parameter in item response theory (IRT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Embretson & Reise, 2000</ref>; see also Supplemental Material A, Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">A1</ref>).

text.text: Because cosine similarity values depend on the embedding model and task, SD values are best interpreted relative to the distribution observed within a given study rather than against a fixed threshold.
IC summarizes the degree of semantic overlap between responses to a candidate question and responses to questions that have already been selected.
At step t, let St denote the set of questions already selected.
IC for candidate question j is computed as the average semantic similarity between responses to question j and responses to the questions in St, averaged across development-sample respondents:
Higher IC indicates greater semantic overlap with previously selected questions; lower IC indicates more distinctive content.
Response length may affect these estimates, but IC is designed to capture overlap in meaning rather than length.
For each construct, questions are ranked using a greedy utility function that combines SD and IC.
Because IC cannot be computed before any questions have been selected, the procedure selects the question with the highest SD first.

At each subsequent step, it scores each remaining question by balancing construct relevance against semantic overlap: qt+1 = arg maxj∉St Uj,d,t Uj,d,t = SDj,d -λICj,t where SD is the raw semantic discrimination value for the candidate question, IC is the raw mean semantic overlap between the candidate question and the questions already selected, and λ determines how semantic overlap is weighted.

Because both SD and IC are entered into the utility function as raw semantic-similarity indices, the scale and interpretation of λ are specific to the embedding model and index implementation used in this study.

Within a given embedding pipeline, standardization is not required for comparing candidate questions or λ conditions because all utilities are computed on the same SD and IC scales; however, λ should not be treated as universally comparable across embedding models or datasets.
Positive values of λ penalize overlap with previously selected questions and therefore favor broader, less redundant coverage.
Values near zero place more weight on construct relevance.
Negative values of λ reward overlap and therefore favor clusters of semantically similar questions, which may be useful when shared trait-relevant signals are more important than breadth of coverage.
The highest-utility question is added next, and the process continues until all questions have been ranked.
Rather than assuming that one λ value is universally optimal, we varied λ to examine whether the method behaved similarly across different weighting choices.

In an initial sensitivity check focused on Conscientiousness and Neuroticism, we examined six λ settings, spanning conditions in which semantic overlap was rewarded to conditions in which it was penalized.

We selected this bounded exploratory range to examine moderate shifts in the relative influence of SD and IC while limiting conditions in which the IC/overlap term would dominate the utility function.
Additional details are provided in Supplemental Material B.
In the final stage, the indices are evaluated to determine whether the resulting shortened Second, we evaluated shortened forms constructed from the ranked question sequences.
For each construct, the greedy procedure produced question rankings under alternative values of λ, thereby varying the weight assigned to semantic overlap.
Shortened forms were defined by taking the first N questions from each ranking and concatenating the corresponding responses in ranked order.
At each interview length, these optimized conditions were compared with the original-order condition at the same length.

For each shortened form, convergence was evaluated using Spearman correlations between the LLM-derived domain scores and the corresponding BFI-2-XS domain scores, thereby focusing on rank-order correspondence between the two assessment methods.
Interdomain structure was examined descriptively using Pearson correlations among the LLM-derived domain scores to summarize linear associations among scores produced by the same scoring method.

Because this analysis focused on the magnitude rather than the direction of heterotrait associations, correlations were converted to absolute values, with lower values indicating clearer separation among domains.
Third, we evaluated measurement efficiency by examining how convergence with the corresponding BFI-2-XS domain changed as additional questions were included.

For each construct and ordering condition, we plotted the correlation between the LLM-derived interview score and the corresponding BFI-2-XS score as a function of interview length, with ranked sequences compared against the original-order sequence.
We also recorded the minimum number of questions required to reach 70%, 80%, and 90% of the condition-specific observed peak convergent validity.

For each trait, embedding model, and ordering condition, the condition-specific observed peak convergent validity was defined as the highest correlation observed across interview lengths N = 1-34, and the threshold value was the smallest N at which the specified proportion of that peak was reached.
We applied our approach to archival data from a chatbot-based narrative personality interview.

text.text: In brief, participants were recruited through a university subject pool and social media advertisements and asked to complete a chatbot-based narrative interview designed to assess personality and the Big Five Inventory-2 Extra-Short Form (BFI-2-XS) (Soto & John, 2017).

text.text: The BFI-2-XS labels two of its domains Negative Emotionality and Open-Mindedness; for consistency with conventional Big Five terminology, we refer to these domains as Neuroticism and Openness, respectively, throughout the manuscript.
The chatbot interview was administered through the Juji conversational AI platform, which presented a structured sequence of 34 open-ended personality interview questions.
The full set of interview questions and the human-rating-referenced domain mapping for each question are presented in Table 1.

text.text: The mapping summarizes how consistently each question was associated with each Big Five domain across the analytic conditions examined by Sylvara et al. (2026), using human ratings as the criterion.

text.text: The present analytic sample was a subset of participants from the larger source dataset from Sun (2021) (N = 455).
text.formatted: The present analytic sample was a subset of participants from the larger source dataset from <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Sun (2021)</ref> (N = 455).

text.text: Since our analyses were conducted at the question level, we retained only participants who provided responses to all interview questions, resulting in a final analytic sample of 303 participants.
The average age of the analytic sample was 21.52 years (SD = 8.00); 62% identified as female, 53.1% as White, 33.0% as Asian, 16.2% as Hispanic or Latinx, and 6.6% as Black or African American.
We first created embeddings for every interview response and for the construct definitions.
For each participant-question pair, the participant's verbatim response was converted into a high-dimensional embedding vector using each pretrained model (DistilBERT and textembedding-3-large).

We also embedded domain-level Big Five descriptions used as constructdefinition anchors for the semantic discrimination index; the exact descriptions are reported in Supplemental Material D, Table D2.
text.formatted: We also embedded domain-level Big Five descriptions used as constructdefinition anchors for the semantic discrimination index; the exact descriptions are reported in Supplemental Material D, Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">D2</ref>.

text.text: The primary output of this step is therefore a set of response-level embeddings, along with one embedding per construct definition.
Although these vectors are not directly interpretable on their own, they serve as the semantic input for all subsequent analyses.
For illustration, Supplemental Material C shows an example of the response-level data structure and the corresponding embedded outputs.
We next used the embeddings to compute SD and the pairwise similarities underlying IC.
SD was computed for each question-trait pair, yielding a question-by-trait table .
Pairwise semantic similarities were then computed between responses elicited by each pair of questions, yielding question-by-question response-similarity matrices.
During greedy ordering, these matrices were used to calculate the step-specific IC of each candidate relative to the questions already selected.
Supplemental Material C illustrates these outputs.
Figure 1 presents SD values across the five Big Five domains for both embedding models, and Table 2 lists the questions with the highest and lowest SD values within each domain.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">1</ref> presents SD values across the five Big Five domains for both embedding models, and Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref> lists the questions with the highest and lowest SD values within each domain.

text.text: Questions that prompted participants to describe behaviors, decisions, or challenges generally had higher SD values than questions focused on factual or contextual information.
For example, the highest-SD questions tended to ask participants to describe enduring tendencies, interpersonal behavior, or major life patterns.
Question 27 ("I'd like you to think about one of your parents or siblings.
Please describe to me how you are similar to or different from them.") showed the highest mean SD in both pipelines (LLM: M = 0.176, rank 1/34; ML: M = 0.755, rank 1/34).

Other high-SD questions, such as Question 20 ("What are your strongest qualities as a friend?") and Question 26 ("How would you describe the personalities of people in the family you grew up in?"), similarly elicited responses about interpersonal style, selfperception, and stable behavioral patterns.

By contrast, Question 1 ("Where are you from?") and Question 2 ("Where did you grow up?") had lower SD values, indicating that their responses were less consistently aligned with the Big Five construct definitions.
In terms of IC, the pairwise response-similarity matrices showed substantial variation in overlap across questions.

Questions such as Q1, Q17, Q29, and Q32 had relatively low average overlap with other questions, whereas several questions concerning school, work, family, and interpersonal experiences showed greater overlap.
The precise pattern differed across embedding models.
These pairwise similarities formed the basis for the step-specific IC values used during question ordering.
Higher IC indicated greater overlap between a candidate question and the questions already selected, rather than a fixed level of redundancy associated with the question itself.
Complete similarity matrices are reported in Supplemental Material E (Tables E2 and E3).
text.formatted: Complete similarity matrices are reported in Supplemental Material E (Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">E2</ref> and <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">E3</ref>).

text.text: We conducted an exploratory sensitivity analysis for Conscientiousness and
Neuroticism across six values of λ (-2, -1, -0.5, 0.5, 1, and 2), spanning overlap-rewarding and overlap-penalizing conditions.
Positive values penalized overlap with previously selected questions, whereas negative values rewarded it.
We then selected λ = 1 and λ = -1 as focal main-text conditions, providing a symmetric comparison between moderate overlap penalization and moderate overlap reward.
This choice was not intended to identify a universally optimal value of λ.

Penalizing overlap generally moved questions contributing more distinctive content earlier in the sequence, but its convergent-validity advantage over rewarding overlap varied by interview length, target domain, and embedding model.
Complete results appear in Supplemental Material A, Table A1.
text.formatted: Complete results appear in Supplemental Material A, Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">A1</ref>.

text.text: After obtaining the optimized question order for each Big Five domain, we computed interview-based trait scores at every possible interview length (N = 1-34).
For each length N, we concatenated the participant's verbatim responses to the first N questions in that domain's optimized sequence into a single text block, preserving the optimized ranked order.

GPT-4o-mini then received this block along with (a) the definition of the focal Big Five domain, (b) the facet definitions (Supplemental Material D, Table D1), and (c) behavioral anchors describing very low, moderate, and very high expressions of each facet (Supplemental Material D, Table D1).
text.formatted: GPT-4o-mini then received this block along with (a) the definition of the focal Big Five domain, (b) the facet definitions (Supplemental Material D, Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">D1</ref>), and (c) behavioral anchors describing very low, moderate, and very high expressions of each facet (Supplemental Material D, Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">D1</ref>).

text.text: For each target domain, GPT-4o-mini rated the three facet-level indicators associated with that domain (e.g., Sociability, Assertiveness, and Energy Level for Extraversion), assigning a single integer score from 1 to 5 to each facet, without explanation.
Facets from other domains were not considered.
Because each domain was evaluated separately, the scoring followed the same domain-specific structure as the question selection.
For each length N, the three facet ratings were averaged to produce a domain-level score.
This score indexed the extent to which the participant's accumulated responses provided evidence for that domain.
These scores were used in the convergent, discriminant, and efficiency analyses.
As shown in Table 3, the λ = 1 redundancy-penalized condition generally yielded descriptively higher convergent correlations than the original-order condition at shorter interview lengths.
text.formatted: As shown in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref>, the λ = 1 redundancy-penalized condition generally yielded descriptively higher convergent correlations than the original-order condition at shorter interview lengths.

text.text: Using ML-based indices, correlations under λ = 1 ranged from .28 to .49 at five questions and from .41 to .57 at seventeen questions.
At N = 34, estimates ranged from .44 to .59, but these full-length differences reflect response ordering rather than question selection because all 34 responses were included.

At N = 5, λ = 1 produced higher validity than the original-order condition for all five traits: Extraversion (.49 vs. .34), Agreeableness (.40 vs. .29), Conscientiousness (.40 vs. .33), Neuroticism (.44 vs. .22), and Openness (.28 vs. .22).
LLMbased indices showed a similar short-form pattern, with validity ranging from .41 to .46 at five questions and from .46 to .60 at seventeen questions.
At N = 34, estimates ranged from .47 to .60 and should be interpreted as order-sensitive full-length scoring results.
In this sample, redundancy-penalized ordering retained substantial convergence with self-reported personality at relatively short interview lengths.
The λ = -1 ordering showed a complementary pattern.
Because IC was implemented as semantic overlap, λ = -1 rewards overlap with previously selected questions rather than penalizing redundancy.
This condition often yielded convergent correlations that were equal to or descriptively higher than those under λ = 1, particularly for Conscientiousness and Neuroticism.
Using ML-based indices, λ = -1 exceeded λ = 1 at N = 17 for both Conscientiousness (.59 vs. .56) and Neuroticism (.59 vs. .56).

At N = 34, all conditions included the same 34 responses, so remaining differences reflect the order in which responses were concatenated and submitted to the LLM rather than differences in selected content.
Corresponding results for the LLM-derived rankings appear in Table 3.
text.formatted: Corresponding results for the LLM-derived rankings appear in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref>.

text.text: Thus, penalizing semantic overlap did not uniformly produce the highest criterion correlations across traits.
Repeated semantic cues may contribute useful trait-related information, but the present analyses do not establish this mechanism.
The questions appearing near the top of the rankings differed across IC weights and embedding models (Table 4).
text.formatted: The questions appearing near the top of the rankings differed across IC weights and embedding models (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">4</ref>).

text.text: With λ = 1, questions selected early tended to have high SD and relatively little overlap with questions already selected.
The two embedding approaches produced different early-question sequences, with only partial overlap among the questions placed near the top.
With λ = -1, questions addressing similar material tended to occur together.
For example, Q26, Q27, and Q28, which concern family similarity and interpersonal relationships, appeared near the top of the same sequence.

These patterns describe differences in question order rather than independently coded differences in content coverage. interview domain scores for the original-order condition and the DistilBERT-based optimized ordering conditions at three interview lengths.
Lower heterotrait correlations indicate clearer construct separation.

Because λ = 1 penalizes semantic overlap under the implemented utility function, shorter-length comparisons most directly assess whether scores based on the first N questions in each optimized sequence show clearer discriminant separation.
Under the original-order condition, the shortest interview length (N = 5) showed substantial cross-trait overlap, with heterotrait correlations ranging from .21 to .62 in magnitude.

Several domain pairs showed relatively strong associations, including E-A (.62), A-C (.59), C-N (.60), and E-O (.56), suggesting limited construct differentiation when only responses to the first five questions in the original interview order were included.
Interdomain correlations generally weakened as interview length increased.

At N = 17, the values ranged from .01 to .54, whereas at N = 34, most off-diagonal values fell below .40, with the largest remaining association observed between Agreeableness and Conscientiousness (.49).
Compared with the original-order condition, the λ = 1 optimized ordering produced weaker interdomain correlations most consistently at shorter interview lengths.
At N = 5, heterotrait correlations ranged from .10 to .35 under λ = 1, compared with .21 to .62 under the original-order condition.
Several associations exceeding .50 under the original-order condition were smaller under λ = 1, including E-A (.62 vs. .33), A-C (.59 vs. .33), C-N (.60 vs. .33), and E-O (.56 vs. .35).
A similar pattern emerged at N = 17, where the largest heterotrait correlation was .40 under λ = 1 and .54 under the original-order condition.
At N = 34, both conditions Results based on the text-embedding-3-large indices showed a broadly similar pattern (Supplemental Material E, Figure E1).
text.formatted: At N = 34, both conditions Results based on the text-embedding-3-large indices showed a broadly similar pattern (Supplemental Material E, Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">E1</ref>).

text.text: Under the original-order condition, heterotrait correlations ranged from .22 to .63 at N = 5 and from .03 to .55 at N = 17.

Under the λ = 1 optimized ordering condition, the corresponding values ranged from .00 to .35 at N = 5 and from .03 to .44 at N = 17, again indicating weaker interdomain associations at the shorter lengths.
Figures 3 and A2 (Supplemental Material A) present efficiency curves for all five traits using indices derived from ML and LLM embeddings.
Higher convergent-validity coefficients at shorter interview lengths were interpreted as greater measurement efficiency.
The dashed horizontal line marks 80% of the largest full-length (N=34) correlation across the plotted conditions.
The curves show how these coefficients changed as questions were added under the redundancy-penalized (λ = 1) and overlap-rewarding (λ = -1) ordering conditions.
In the ML-based results, Extraversion reached r = .49 at five questions and .56 at ten.
At five questions, λ = 1 yielded higher coefficients than λ = -1 for Agreeableness (.40 vs. .26) and Neuroticism (.44 vs. .39), although λ = -1 was higher for Neuroticism at longer lengths.
For Conscientiousness, λ = -1 was slightly higher at N = 5 and higher at N = 17, whereas λ = 1 was higher at N = 10.
Openness coefficients were similar across conditions and increased gradually with interview length.
The LLM-based results showed a broadly similar but more trait-specific pattern.
At five questions, λ = 1 yielded higher validity than λ = -1 for Extraversion (.46 vs. .43), Agreeableness (.41 vs. .40), and especially Openness (.42 vs. .27).
In contrast, λ = -1 produced stronger early or mid-length validity for Conscientiousness and Neuroticism.
For Neuroticism, λ = -1 reached .58 by seventeen questions, compared with .47 under λ = 1.
These findings suggest that the relative performance of the two ordering conditions varied across traits and interview lengths.
To assess the practical implications of these patterns, we compared the λ = 1 and λ = -1 optimized orders with same-length versions of the original question order at N = 5 and N = 10 (Figure 4).
text.formatted: To assess the practical implications of these patterns, we compared the λ = 1 and λ = -1 optimized orders with same-length versions of the original question order at N = 5 and N = 10 (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">4</ref>).

text.text: In the LLM-embedding pipeline, at least one optimized condition generally yielded descriptively higher convergent correlations than the original order at short lengths, although the observed gains varied by trait, interview length, and λ value.

At N = 5, λ = 1 produced larger gains for Extraversion, Agreeableness, and Openness, consistent with the possibility that placing less semantically overlapping questions earlier was advantageous for these traits.
For Agreeableness and Openness, the gains were smaller at N = 10 because the original order recovered substantial validity with additional questions.

In contrast, λ = -1 produced larger gains for Conscientiousness and Neuroticism, consistent with the possibility that semantic overlap preserved useful trait-relevant signals, particularly for Conscientiousness (Δr = .13 and .07 at N = 5 and 10, respectively) and Neuroticism (Δr = .23 and .29, respectively).

Thus, λ functions as a tuning parameter: positive values prioritize less redundant coverage, whereas negative values may preserve overlapping content that strengthens convergent validity for some traits.
We also estimated how many questions were needed to recover 70%, 80%, and 90% of each trait's condition-specific observed peak convergent validity across N = 1-34 (Table 5).
text.formatted: We also estimated how many questions were needed to recover 70%, 80%, and 90% of each trait's condition-specific observed peak convergent validity across N = 1-34 (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_4">5</ref>).

text.text: This analysis asks how many questions are needed to reach a specified proportion of the best observed correlation within each efficiency curve.
Across embedding models and weighting parameters, 80% of peak validity was typically reached using only a small fraction of the full 34-question interview.
All conditions reached the 80% threshold within 3 to 12 questions, and many did so within the first third of the interview.
Reaching 90% of peak validity required more questions, ranging from 6 to 20 questions across traits and conditions.

Thus, the optimized orderings often recovered most of the attainable validity well before the full interview was administered, although the number of questions needed for near-peak validity varied by trait and ordering condition.
This study introduces two response-based semantic indices for evaluating openended interview questions based on participants' narrative responses.

Building on prior work in item reduction and text-based psychometric analysis (e.g., Hinkin, 1995; Kilmen & Bulut, 2025; Milano et al., 2025; Van Iddekinge et al., 2005), we show that response-based semantic indices can identify questions that are construct-relevant while also varying in the degree to which they provide overlapping or distinctive information.
text.formatted: Building on prior work in item reduction and text-based psychometric analysis (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Hinkin, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Kilmen & Bulut, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Milano et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Van Iddekinge et al., 2005)</ref>, we show that response-based semantic indices can identify questions that are construct-relevant while also varying in the degree to which they provide overlapping or distinctive information.

text.text: Optimized ranked-order conditions generally yielded descriptively higher short-form convergent correlations than the original-order conditions, with the largest observed gains at shorter interview lengths.

Orderings that emphasized broader, less redundant coverage generally yielded lower interdomain correlations, consistent with clearer construct separation, whereas orderings that preserved semantically overlapping questions sometimes yielded higher convergent correlations.
Under the implemented utility function, these patterns corresponded to the redundancy-penalized (λ = 1) and overlap-rewarding (λ = -1) conditions, respectively.

These results suggest that participants' narrative responses provide rich information to support more effective item selection and sequencing, while also showing that the observed gains reflect both which responses are included and the order in which they are presented to the scoring model.
This research extends prior work in two ways.

Most prior work on shortening assessments has focused on structured scales, using classical psychometric criteria such as itemtotal correlations, factor loadings, or IRT-based information functions (Embretson & Reise, 2000; Hinkin, 1995).
text.formatted: Most prior work on shortening assessments has focused on structured scales, using classical psychometric criteria such as itemtotal correlations, factor loadings, or IRT-based information functions <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Embretson & Reise, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Hinkin, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: We adapt similar item-analytic logic to open-ended interviews, where responses are expressed in natural language rather than fixed response categories.
Existing semantic approaches typically evaluate item text itself (e.g., Kilmen & Bulut, 2025; Milano et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Existing semantic approaches typically evaluate item text itself (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Kilmen & Bulut, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Milano et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, the present approach evaluates interview questions based on the semantic properties of participants' responses, which better reflect how questions function in practice.
This distinction matters because interview items cannot be understood from wording alone; their value depends on the narratives they elicit.
Interview development often depends on expert judgment and repeated revision (e.g., Van Iddekinge et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Interview development often depends on expert judgment and repeated revision (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Van Iddekinge et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: The present results suggest that SD and IC can provide an additional source of evidence when reviewing interview questions.
They can help identify questions that tend to elicit construct-relevant responses and questions whose responses overlap with content elicited elsewhere.
This may be useful when a full manual review is not practical.
The same information can inform decisions about shortening an interview.
The indices are not intended to replace expert judgment, but they can help practitioners compare candidate questions and decide which ones should be retained, revised, or removed.
This may be particularly useful in highvolume hiring, longitudinal studies, and other settings in which lengthy interviews can reduce response quality.
SD and IC may also support periodic review of existing interview protocols.
As more responses are collected, organizations can examine whether some questions have become repetitive or function differently as the applicant pool changes.
These analyses can help guide later revisions to the interview.
Personality traits can be inferred from natural language when linguistic indicators are validated against established psychological measures (Park et al., 2015; Tay et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Personality traits can be inferred from natural language when linguistic indicators are validated against established psychological measures <ref type="bibr">(Park et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Tay et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The results here also point to several methodological issues that arise when language models are used at multiple stages of a measurement procedure.
A key concern is common method effects when language models are used both to evaluate questions and to score responses.
Here, embeddings informed SD and IC, whereas a language model inferred personality traits.

Observed gains may therefore partly reflect shared model-sensitive features across selection and scoring: questions eliciting responses that language models can more readily interpret may be preferentially selected.
More generally, common method bias can inflate associations when variables are derived using similar measurement or analytic procedures (Podsakoff et al., 2003 (Podsakoff et al., , 2012)).
text.formatted: More generally, common method bias can inflate associations when variables are derived using similar measurement or analytic procedures <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Podsakoff et al., 2003</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Podsakoff et al., , 2012))</ref>.

text.text: We examined this possibility in two ways.
First, we computed the semantic indices using two distinct embedding approaches, DistilBERT and text-embedding-3-large, to assess whether the observed patterns were similar across representations.
Second, we evaluated convergent validity against participants' self-reported Big Five scores from the BFI-2-XS.
Thus, the evaluation incorporated an external psychological criterion rather than relying solely on consistency between model-based analyses.
Prior work also shows that language in open-ended responses can relate to personality traits when evaluated against external criteria (Park et al., 2015; Tay et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Prior work also shows that language in open-ended responses can relate to personality traits when evaluated against external criteria <ref type="bibr">(Park et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Tay et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Future research should evaluate these effects directly by comparing model-based scores with human ratings or testing whether question-selection patterns replicate across scoring methods.
Such comparisons would clarify whether observed gains reflect construct-relevant psychological signals or features specific to a particular analytic approach.
A related concern is that questions with higher semantic discrimination (SD) may simply elicit longer responses, providing richer linguistic input for embedding-based analyses.
To examine this, we conducted a response-length sensitivity analysis (Supplemental Material F, Figure F1).
text.formatted: To examine this, we conducted a response-length sensitivity analysis (Supplemental Material F, Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">F1</ref>).

text.text: Higher-SD questions tended to elicit longer responses, although the strength of this association depended on the embedding model.
For LLM-based embeddings, correlations between SD and mean response length were modest to moderate across domains (r = .25-.50).
For ML-based embeddings, the associations were stronger (r = .75-.78), indicating that response length may contribute more substantially to SD in that representation space.

After residualizing SD with respect to response length and regenerating the greedy question ordering, overlap with the original rankings varied by model and number of questions, with greater stability for LLMbased rankings than for ML-based rankings.
These results suggest that SD is not reducible to verbosity alone, but response length should be treated as an important sensitivity concern, especially for ML-based embeddings.
The value of λ determines how the ranking treats questions that elicit similar responses.
Because IC is defined as semantic overlap, λ = 1 moves such questions down the ranking when their content is already represented, whereas λ = -1 moves them up.
Thus, λ determines how much repeated semantic content is retained in the shortened interview.
Although the present analyses do not estimate internal consistency, the underlying design problem is familiar.

A set of highly similar items may produce high internal consistency but represent the construct too narrowly. Cronbach and Meehl (1955) cautioned that internal consistency supports construct validity only when the theory calls for strongly related items and that high internal consistency may sometimes lower validity.
text.formatted: A set of highly similar items may produce high internal consistency but represent the construct too narrowly. <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Cronbach and Meehl (1955)</ref> cautioned that internal consistency supports construct validity only when the theory calls for strongly related items and that high internal consistency may sometimes lower validity.

text.text: The same tension arises here.
Several questions covering related material may provide useful repeated evidence about a trait, but they may also take the place of questions that sample other parts of the domain.
The results suggest that both possibilities occurred.
At shorter interview lengths, the λ = 1 condition generally showed descriptively higher convergent correlations and weaker heterotrait correlations than the baseline condition.
Accordingly, the lower semantic overlap observed under λ = 1 was not accompanied by lower convergent correlations at shorter interview lengths.
Yet λ = -1 matched or exceeded λ = 1 for some traits, especially Conscientiousness and Neuroticism.
For these traits, related prompts may have reinforced a common trait signal rather than simply repeated the same information.
IC alone cannot distinguish useful repetition from unnecessary redundancy.
No value of λ should be treated as best in general.
Positive values are most relevant when the aim is to reduce repeated content and leave room for broader coverage.
Values near zero or below may be useful when related prompts are expected to strengthen measurement within a narrower domain.
Useful values may also differ across embedding models because models represent semantic similarity differently.
In new applications, the rankings should be evaluated against convergent and discriminant relations and reviewed for the content they retain.
Independent content coding is still needed to determine whether one ordering covers the construct more broadly than another.
The present results show how λ changes the selected sequence; they do not identify an optimal setting.
Convergence with established self-report measures such as the BFI-2-XS provides an initial benchmark for evaluating shortened interviews.

New measurement approaches should correspond to established measures of the same constructs; otherwise, whether they capture the same underlying traits is unclear (Campbell & Fiske, 1959; Cronbach & Meehl, 1955).
text.formatted: New measurement approaches should correspond to established measures of the same constructs; otherwise, whether they capture the same underlying traits is unclear <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Campbell & Fiske, 1959;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Cronbach & Meehl, 1955)</ref>.

text.text: Meaningful correlations with the BFI-2-XS therefore indicate that optimized interviews retain trait-relevant variance as their length is reduced.
Interview-based assessments need not be redundant with self-report questionnaires.

Multitrait-multimethod research indicates that different methods capture partially distinct variance arising from response format, cognitive processing, and contextualized behavioral recall (Campbell & Fiske, 1959; Paulhus & Vazire, 2007).
text.formatted: Multitrait-multimethod research indicates that different methods capture partially distinct variance arising from response format, cognitive processing, and contextualized behavioral recall <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Campbell & Fiske, 1959;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Paulhus & Vazire, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Open-ended interviews elicit narratives, behavioral examples, and situational context, whereas choice-based questionnaires rely largely on abstract self-evaluations.
Moderate cross-method correlations are therefore expected; extremely high correlations would instead suggest redundancy.
Our goal was not to reproduce self-report scores but to determine whether shortened interviews retained construct-relevant personality information within a narrative response format.
Because the archival dataset lacked external criteria, we could not evaluate incremental predictive validity over self-report.
Future research should examine whether optimized interview sequences predict relevant outcomes beyond traditional choice-based questionnaires.
One concern is that embedding models may not represent all forms of language equally well.
Because these models are trained on large text corpora, their representations can reflect the linguistic and cultural patterns that are most common in those data.

In an interview context, this means that some ways of describing personality-relevant experiences may be treated as more typical or more semantically aligned than others, even when the underlying behavior is similar (Bender et al., 2021; Mehrabi et al., 2021).
text.formatted: In an interview context, this means that some ways of describing personality-relevant experiences may be treated as more typical or more semantically aligned than others, even when the underlying behavior is similar <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Bender et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Mehrabi et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In this setting, bias would matter if the model identifies some ways of describing traitrelevant behavior more readily than others.

For example, responses from non-native speakers or individuals from different cultural backgrounds may express personality-relevant behaviors using linguistic forms that are less typical in the model's training data.
If not carefully examined, such effects could lead to systematic differences in how interview responses are interpreted across groups.
These concerns are closely related to established psychometric approaches to measurement fairness.

In traditional test development, fairness is often evaluated using Differential Item Functioning (DIF) analyses, which examine whether items operate differently across demographic groups (Millsap, 2011; Zumbo, 1999).
text.formatted: In traditional test development, fairness is often evaluated using Differential Item Functioning (DIF) analyses, which examine whether items operate differently across demographic groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Millsap, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Zumbo, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Similar checks will be needed before these procedures are used in settings where subgroup differences matter.

For example, future studies could examine whether interview items selected by the proposed method exhibit differential measurement properties across language groups, cultural backgrounds, or other demographic characteristics.
A next step is to treat narrative responses as multidimensional rather than optimize each trait in isolation.
Open-ended accounts rarely isolate constructs, and single questions often tap multiple domains at once.

Although this study optimized items separately for each construct, work on construct representation and multidimensional measurement (Borsboom, 2005; Embretson & Reise, 2000) shows that item functioning must be understood within a broader latent space.
text.formatted: Although this study optimized items separately for each construct, work on construct representation and multidimensional measurement <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Borsboom, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Embretson & Reise, 2000)</ref> shows that item functioning must be understood within a broader latent space.

text.text: Future models should estimate information across constructs jointly, quantify crossdomain overlap, and use optimization criteria that balance multiple goals.
That structure would be closer to how interviews are usually interpreted, where the same answer may inform more than one trait.
A generalizable multi-construct utility framework, similar to multidimensional IRT in adaptive testing, could help guide question ordering in more complex assessment settings.
The same logic may also apply outside narrative interviews.
Any assessment that asks people to respond in their own words produces text that can be evaluated for construct relevance and redundancy.
The details would likely vary by format.
A situational judgment question, for example, may create a different kind of overlap than a life-history interview question.
Future work should therefore examine which parts of SD and IC generalize across text-based assessments and which need to be adapted to the task.
Future research should explore adaptive interviewing procedures.
The present analyses also treat the question order as fixed once it is selected.
In practice, however, interviews unfold one response at a time.
A respondent may provide rich evidence about a domain early in the interview, whereas another respondent may not.
This creates a natural opening for adaptive administration.
One possible design would begin with a small common set of questions and then select later questions based on what has already been said.

Such a system could use sample-level SD estimates to identify questions likely to be construct relevant, but it would need a respondentlevel version of IC to avoid asking questions that elicit the same content again.
The current IC index was estimated from development-sample responses, so it cannot be used for that purpose without modification.
Our approach has several limitations.
Alternative sequences were evaluated through post hoc simulation of archival responses collected under a single fixed order.
This analysis therefore assumes that participants would give the same responses if the questions were presented in a different order.

Open-ended interviews, however, are path-dependent: earlier questions shape context and rapport, whereas later responses may reflect fatigue, prior disclosures, and the cognitive or emotional demands of preceding questions.
Reordering observed responses cannot capture these dynamics.
Simulated gains should therefore be interpreted cautiously because optimized sequences may perform differently in live interviews.
Gains may shrink if certain questions reduce engagement when placed earlier or increase if diagnostic questions appear when attention and narrative elaboration are highest.

Empirical studies directly manipulating question order are essential to determine whether optimized sequences alter participant engagement, response depth, or construct expression, and to verify whether the observed efficiency gains generalize to prospective samples.
The semantic indices also inherit the strengths and limitations of the embedding models used to generate them.
Text models reflect patterns in their training data and differ in how they weight themes, emotions, and demographic signals.
SD and IC are therefore not self-validating metrics.
Their interpretation depends on clear construct definitions, a coherent facet structure, and substantive judgment about the intended construct.
Text-based methods expand the tools available for evaluating interview questions but do not replace theory-driven reasoning.
A further limitation concerns fairness and algorithmic bias in embedding-based assessment.

Because language models are trained on large text corpora, their representations may reflect dominant linguistic conventions and fail to fully capture meaning conveyed through regional dialects, subcultural idioms, or second-language use.

The proposed indices are used to select and order interview questions, not to score respondents.
Evaluating shortened forms, however, requires construct-level interview scores.

In the present case study, participant-level interviewer ratings of the interview responses were not available, so we used an LLM-based scoring procedure to generate domain scores from participants' accumulated responses at each interview length.

This choice follows prior work showing that AI-and LLM-based systems can score open-ended personality interview responses in a standardized manner(Speer et al., 2026; Sylvara et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This choice follows prior work showing that AI-and LLM-based systems can score open-ended personality interview responses in a standardized manner<ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Speer et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Sylvara et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Yan et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These scores were used only to evaluate convergent validity, discriminant structure, and measurement efficiency of the shortened forms.
Domain scores were generated through the OpenAI Chat Completions API using the model alias gpt-4o-mini with temperature set to 0.
Complete prompt and implementation details are provided in Supplemental Material D.The evaluation proceeded in three parts.
First, we examined question-level patterns in SD and semantic overlap.
SD was computed for each question and target domain under each embedding model.
We also computed pairwise semantic similarities between responses elicited by different questions.
These similarities formed the basis for the step-specific IC values used during question ordering.
The outputs of this stage were question-by-domain SD values and question-by-question response-similarity matrices.

During ordering, higher IC indicated greater overlap between a candidate question and the questions already selected, whereas lower IC indicated more distinctive content relative to the current selected set.
Figure2presents the absolute values of Pearson correlations among the LLM-derived linguistic form to cultural content.
Respondents from different backgrounds may associate the same question with different experiences, obligations, relationships, or achievements.
Questions about work, family, friendship, or challenge may therefore elicit different content across groups, even when responses are equally thoughtful and informative.
Interview responses are also shaped by their interpersonal context.
Disclosure, level of detail, and the examples treated as relevant may vary with rapport, perceived evaluation pressure, interviewer behavior, and expectations about appropriate responses.
Embedding-based indices may not capture these differences when one pattern of response content is treated as more typical or construct-relevant than another.

Future research should therefore examine the stability of semantic indices across linguistic and cultural groups and interviewer contexts, particularly in high-stakes assessment settings.ConclusionWe propose a semantic approach based on two indices (i.e., semantic discrimination and information coverage) to evaluate how interview questions function in narrative assessments.
SD tells us whether a question tends to elicit trait-relevant content, whereas IC tells us whether the question adds new content or repeats what earlier questions already elicited.
Our approach can help identify high-value questions and preserve convergent validity with self-reported construct scores when interviews are shortened.
These results suggest that response embeddings can serve as item-level evidence for refining open-ended assessments.
